title: The Count
passages:
Nia clicked the blister pack open and shut. Three doses. She counted again. Three.

Teo’s breathing came from under her coat, shallow and wet. She didn’t look up when Wren crouched on the step beside her.

“You want me to check that harness?” Wren asked.

“I want you to keep the Caller burning and keep your hands off my pack.”

Wren held up both palms. “Relax. I’m not the one who ran a cold-box by hand for a year while starving in a tower. I’m just saying your chest strap looks twisted.”

Nia looked. It wasn’t. She pulled it tighter anyway. “Mind your slate.”

“Mine’s got one play left and a dead woman’s voice on it,” Wren said. “Yours is medicine math. I don’t know which one’s going to kill you first.”

From the step below, Mara said, “Fifty-one.”

Nia’s jaw locked. She tilted the pack toward the dim light from the warden’s box. Teo weighed twenty kilos. One dose lasted twelve hours if she stretched it, six if she didn’t. The storm would hold the channel shut for months. She did the math and came up empty.

“Fifty-two,” Mara said.

Above them, the lock teeth of the Kettle’s low gate ground together, iron on iron, closing the channel to the surge. Water slapped the pilings. Somewhere below the step, Mara’s boots swung over the dark, hollow and counting.

Nia shifted Teo against her side. He was warm. That was the only good thing she could say about him. He coughed and didn’t wake.

“Fifty-three,” Mara said.

Nia wiped her thumb on her pants. “Seventy’s going to come,” she said. “Then what? You start over? You stop breathing?”

Mara didn’t answer. She never answered. She just counted, her voice flat and even, the only clock they had left now that the gate had sealed.

The final tooth dropped with a thud that rang up through the box step. Silence settled, thick and cold. Nia held her breath for it. When nothing else came, she let it out.

Wren nudged her shoulder with her boot. “You gonna dive that trunk anyway?”

Nia looked at the three blister packs, at Mara’s blank eyes, and up at the shutter where Sol had stood with a forfeit bond and no berth left to sell. “I have to,” she said.

“Fifty-three,” Mara said again.

Footsteps rang on the metal stair behind them. Heavy. Wet. Dey.

Nia didn’t turn. She kept her eyes on Mara, who sat two steps down with her hood up and her boots swinging over the dark. The lock teeth had finished grinding. The channel was shut. Only Mara’s voice remained, ticking upward like a counter in a dead machine.

“Fifty-four.”

Nia’s fingers tightened on Teo’s blister pack. Three doses. She had counted them a dozen times already.

“Fifty-five.”

Between numbers, Mara said, “Thirty-eight.”

Then: “Fifty-six.”

Nia went still. She had heard that number before. Not in Mara’s count, but in the first play on Salas’s slate—Mara’s voice, calm and unfamiliar, directing a diver to a second sealed pocket below the pharmacy at Mercy General. The service trunk. Thirty-eight meters under the Line, where the water was cold enough to steal memory and the hours never came back.

Nia looked up at the warden’s shutter. Sol had stood there with a forfeit bond and no berth left to sell. Inside, Quill’s book was open to the full count: forty-one names, no empty berths except four-eleven, held by Mara Vos, paid in mint gold.

Mint gold. Pre-drown currency, heavy and stamped, the kind of money that bought a place on the high arcology before storm season. Quill had written it into her book as payment. But Mara was down here on the wet step, hollow and counting, not up in the gatehouse handing over coins. The gold wasn’t in the warden’s box. It was still down there, in the trunk, under the Line, where Mara had said it was.

“Thirty-eight,” Nia said quietly.

Dey shifted his weight behind her. His breath rattled in his chest. He didn’t speak.

From below, Mara said, “Fifty-seven.”

Nia touched the seal of the service hatch at her feet. Cold water seeped around its rim. The trunk was closed, dogged down, waiting. And somewhere at thirty-eight meters, beneath the water that was already closing over the Kettle, sat enough mint gold to buy a berth—maybe more than one. Enough for Dey’s papers. Enough to keep the Marrow afloat.

She looked at the three blister packs in her hand, then at the dark hatch. The count was still going up. Mara had not stopped. But Nia knew where the next number led.

“Nia,” Dey said. His voice scraped against the step. “Quill’s down. She sent the order up through the speaking tube. Dive the debt off or the Factor takes you.”

Nia didn’t look at him. She kept her eyes on the dark hatch. “He’s not diving anything.”

“She said the indenture’s due in three hours. Papers come due before the storm turns. He either goes under or he goes to the barge.”

Dey coughed, wet and racking. He spat onto the metal step. “I can hold my breath long enough,” he said. His voice was thin, stripped of its usual edge. “Thirty-eight meters. I’ve done worse.”

“You gave your scrubber to Teo,” Nia said. “Your lungs haven’t cleared since. You go below the Line and you won’t come up whole.”

“Whole is overrated.”

Wren stood and brushed her knees off. “Below a certain depth, the pressure takes your memory. You forget your sister’s face. You forget why you’re down there. You forget how to breathe back up.”

“I remember enough,” Dey said. He pushed off the frame and took a step toward the hatch. His knees buckled. Nia caught his arm before he fell.

“Let go,” he said.

“No.”

“Nia,” he said, quieter now. “My papers. They take me to the Factor’s keeping, I never see the Marrow again. I never buy my freedom.”

“Then we find another way,” she said. But she knew there wasn’t one. The book was full. The berths were sold. The only person who knew the trunk was Mara, who was counting upward from one and wouldn’t stop.

Mara said, “Fifty-eight.”

Dey looked at her, then back at Nia. “You gonna go down there?”

Nia didn’t answer. She looked at the blister pack. Three doses. Teo was breathing under her coat, wet and shallow.

“Fifty-nine.”

“If you go,” Dey said, “you’re spending memory you can’t afford.”

“If I don’t go,” Nia said, “you lose your freedom and Teo loses his medicine. Pick which one you can live with.”

Dey opened his mouth, then shut it. Water dripped from his chin onto the step. He looked at Mara, who sat with her boots swinging over the dark, still counting.

“Sixty.”

The warden’s shutter cracked open above them. Sol’s face appeared in the gap, gray and tired. Her hand was flat on the sill.

“The Factor doesn’t take children,” Sol said. “But he takes indentured divers. Dey, you hear me? You don’t take that line.”

“I don’t have a choice,” Dey said.

“You always have a choice,” Sol said. “You just don’t like the ones you’re given.”

The shutter slammed shut. Only Mara’s voice remained, climbing upward into the cold.

Nia stood, tucking the blister pack into her coat. “Then I’ll take the line.”

Dey grabbed her wrist. “Your scrubber’s half-spent. The cartridge—that’s the thing that scrubs the bad air out so you can breathe it again—won’t last to thirty-eight.”

“Then I’ll surface before it quits,” Nia said.

“You won’t make it. Eight meters short, you’ll be sucking seawater and forgetting your own name.”

“Sixty-one,” Mara said.

Nia pulled her arm free. “Watch me.”

She stepped toward the hatch. Dey didn’t let go.

Wren didn't move toward the hatch. She moved toward Mara.

The woman sat two steps down, hood drawn, boots swinging over the black water. Her lips moved without pause. *Sixty-two. Sixty-three.* The counting was the only thing keeping her tethered. Wren had seen hollow divers before — eyes open, voices working, nothing behind them but the pressure's slow erase. She knelt on the wet metal beside Mara's dangling feet and waited for a gap in the numbers.

*Sixty-four. Sixty-five.*

Wren reached into her coat and pulled the slate. Salas's drowned recorder, barnacled and salt-cracked, its playback head still gummed with grease from the pharmacy pocket. She thumbed the contact clean on her sleeve, pressed the play stud, and held it close to Mara's ear.

Static hissed. Then Mara's own voice, thinner than the woman on the step, speaking words Wren had never heard: *No diver already hollow shall be sent below the Line. The forgetting takes what little remains. This order stands until countermanded by the Caller.*

The recording clicked off.

Wren sat back on her heels. The slate felt heavier than its weight. She looked at Mara's profile — the hollow cheeks, the eyes fixed on nothing, the mouth still shaping numbers. *Sixty-six. Sixty-seven.*

"Rule's on the slate," Wren said. Her voice came out flatter than she meant. "Mara's own voice. Fourteen months ago. She ordered it herself."

Nia stood frozen with one foot on the hatch coaming, Dey's hand still clamped on her wrist. Dey's breathing had gone ragged, each inhale a whistle through damaged airways. He stared at the slate in Wren's hand like it had bitten her.

"She *made* the rule," Nia said. "And she's the only one who knows the trunk."

"She's hollow," Wren said. "The rule says hollow divers don't go below. The pressure finishes what the dark started. You send her down, you don't get her back. You don't get the cache either — she forgets where it is halfway there."

*Sixty-eight. Sixty-nine.*

Dey's grip on Nia's wrist loosened. He wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. "So that's it. The only person who knows the way is the one person who can't go."

"Looks like," Wren said. She tucked the slate back into her coat. "Which leaves somebody still whole."

Nia looked down at her own hands. The blister pack bulged in her coat pocket. Teo's weight against her side. The hatch gaped at her feet, cold water seeping around the dogging clamps.

"Seventy," Mara said.

The number hung in the cold air. Nia's jaw worked. She looked at Dey, at his shaking hands and his gray lips, then at Wren, and finally at the dark water below the step.

"Me," Nia said. "I'm whole."

Nia didn't wait for permission. She vaulted the rail and hit the Marrow's deck at a run, her boots ringing on wet steel. The boat sat lashed in the gate's lee, fenders screaming against the pilings as the surge tested the lines. Bayo stood at the wheel, bandaged hands white-knuckled on the spokes, watching the water climb the ladder rungs. He didn't turn when she blew past him toward the companionway.

The rebreather rack was forward, bolted to the bulkhead beside the drum. Three units. One stripped for parts, one with a cracked faceplate from the pharmacy pocket, and the one Salas had worn — scratched, salt-crusted, but holding pressure when Wren tested it yesterday. Nia grabbed it, thumbs finding the canister release by feel. She cracked the housing. The CO2 cartridge inside was gray-green, the indicator strip faded to the color of old bruises. Half-spent. Maybe a little more. She snapped it shut anyway.

"Vos." Bayo's voice from the ladder well. He'd followed. "That canister's rated for forty minutes at thirty meters. You've got thirty-eight to reach and thirty-eight to come back. The math doesn't close."

"Math never closes down there," Nia said. She slung the harness over her shoulders, cinched the waist strap, checked the quick-release. "It buys time. That's all I need."

She climbed back up the companionway, the rebreather banging her hip. On deck, Salas stood by the drum, hood up against the wind, a coil of synthetic line spooled over one shoulder. He didn't look at her. He hadn't spoken since surfacing, not until he'd said Bayo's name over the comms. But he held the line out when she reached him — a silent offer, the bitter end already spliced with a locking carabiner.

Nia clipped it to her chest D-ring. The gate snapped loud in the wind.

"Teo," she called down the companionway.

The boy appeared at the hatch, wrapped in a blanket three sizes too big. His eyes were huge, dark circles bruised beneath them. He clutched the Caller's battery pack to his chest — the heavy lithium brick that kept the bell's single tone alive in the drowned hospital tower, the only thing Mara had tended for fourteen months.

"Keep it burning," Nia said. She crouched, brought her face level with his. "The Caller. You watch the charge. When the light blinks red, you swap the spare from the locker. You don't let it go dark. Not for a second. You hear me?"

Teo's throat worked. He nodded once, sharp.

"Good." She pressed her forehead to his, brief and hard. "I'm coming back. You hold the line up here."

She turned to the rail. The water below was black, the Kettle's floodlights cutting cones that vanished into silt. Somewhere down there, the service trunk waited at thirty-eight meters, dogged shut and silent. Mint gold. A child's coat. Enough to buy berths, burn papers, keep them whole.

Dey stood on the step below the warden's box, one hand braced on the railing. His chest heaved. He didn't try to stop her this time.

Wren sat beside Mara on the wet metal, slate dark in her lap. Mara's voice rose into the wind. *Seventy-one. Seventy-two.*

Nia put her regulator in, bit down on the silicone mouthpiece, and took her first breath of scrubbed air. It tasted of copper and old plastic. She exhaled, watched the bubbles climb the faceplate, and swung her legs over the rail.

"Seventy-three," Mara said.

Nia dropped.

The cold hit her like a fist. She kicked down, equalizing on every third kick, the line paying out smooth from Salas's hands above. Ten meters. The floodlights faded. Fifteen. The pressure built behind her ears, familiar and patient. Twenty. Her breath sounded loud in her ears — *hiss, click, hiss, click* — the rebreather's solenoid adding oxygen, the canister stripping carbon dioxide. The indicator on her wrist read green. For now.

"Twenty meters," she called up the line. Her voice came strange through the mouthpiece, muffled and thin.

Bayo's answer came through the comms, tinny and tight. "Copy. Drum's free. Take your time."

*Liar,* she thought. *There's no time left.*

She kicked deeper. Twenty-five. Thirty. The green light on her wrist flickered — once, twice — and settled on amber.

The air in her mouth turned thick. Sour. Each inhale dragged resistance through the canister like sucking through wet cloth. The CO2 wasn't scrubbing clean anymore. She could feel it building behind her eyes, a dull pressure that had nothing to do with depth.

"Thirty meters," she said. Her voice cracked. "Canister's failing."

"Push or pull?" Bayo asked.

Nia looked down. The service trunk's upper seal was a darker shadow in the gloom, eight meters below. Eight meters of cold and pressure and forgetting. The amber light on her wrist pulsed like a heartbeat.

She checked her depth gauge. Thirty meters even. The scrubber was dying. The cache was eight meters deeper.

"Push," she said.

She pushed.

The trunk's mouth came up out of the murk all at once, a black square the floodlights couldn't reach, ringed by a coaming — the raised lip around a hatch — furred soft green with a year of growth. Two covers sat stacked inside it, an outer seal and an inner one behind, both dogged down. The dogging clamps were steel lugs, six to a cover, that bit the rim and held the sea out. Salt had half-welded the first one shut.

Nia braced a boot on the coaming and put both gloves on the lug. It didn't move. She reversed, cracked the grit loose, and threw her shoulder into it. The clamp spun free with a shriek she felt in her back teeth.

"Thirty meters," she called up the line. "At the outer seal. One lug off."

"Beautiful," Bayo said, warm as bathwater. "You're a natural, Nia. Run a hundred of these myself, you couldn't be in better—"

"Save it." She got the second lug. The third. Her breath was coming harder now, each pull through the canister like drawing air through a wet sock. The amber light on her wrist held steady, the color of a warning nobody had heeded yet.

Four lugs. Five. The last one fought her, and when it gave, the outer cover swung in on its hinge and the sea leaned through the gap — the trunk's own water, still and black and older than the storm up top.

"Outer seal's open," she said, and her voice came back thin, a stranger's voice in her own mouthpiece. "Going for the inner."

"Copy. Drum's holding steady. Take all the time you need."

"There isn't any." She got her gloves on the inner cover's first clamp.

This one turned easy. Too easy. The salt hadn't set on it the way it had on the outer seal — no green furred over the threads, no year of growth in the gap. The clamp gave at a touch, and the second, and the third, all of them loose as if someone had spun them off not long ago and never dogged them back down.

Nia went still on the coaming.

"Talk to me, Vos," Bayo said.

"Somebody's been here." She said it slow, working it out as she went. "The inner seal's been opened. Recent. These lugs are clean — no salt, no growth. The outer was welded shut a year and the inner's loose as a hinge. Whoever it was came through the outer and never closed either one behind them."

The line stayed quiet a moment. Then, tinny and careful: "You sure."

"I'm looking at it." She was. Four bright lugs in a ring, bare steel where a year should've buried them. Somebody had come this way with hands, and hands meant air, and air meant they'd made it this deep and back — or they hadn't, and the trunk had kept whatever was left.

She thought of Mara up top, boots swinging, saying thirty-eight between the numbers like she'd left it there herself. Paid mint gold into a book for a berth, and never come up to the box to hand it over. Still down here in the cold, or gone somewhere the pressure takes everything and gives nothing back.

"Nia." Bayo again, and the warmth had thinned out of it now. "That trunk's a shaft. You put the last cover off, there's no deck under it, no shelf — just the drop, straight down to whatever Mara left. You go in there, I can't see you and the drum can't feel you but through the line."

"I know what a shaft is." She set her hand on the inner cover, ready to swing it the rest of the way wide.

"Then know this. Somebody opened this and left it open. That's not a person in a hurry. That's a person who meant to come back and didn't."

Nia looked down through the gap she'd made. Below the loose inner seal the water fell away into a dark the floodlights had already lost, eight meters of it, straight and black, down to the gold and the coat and the answer to why a woman would give away her air, her hours, her name and still not stop counting.

"Then I'll be the one who comes back," she said, and swung the seal wide onto the drop.

The drop swallowed her.

Nia kicked down the shaft, the line feeding smooth from Salas's hands above, each pull of the rebreather dragging heavier than the last. The amber light on her wrist pulsed steady — *warning, warning, warning* — and the air in her mouth tasted like copper pennies and old exhaust. Thirty-one meters. The pressure behind her eyes wasn't depth anymore. It was CO2 building in her blood, screaming at her brain to breathe faster, deeper, *now*.

Thirty-two. The shaft walls were concrete, streaked with rust and something darker, scored by years of current. No handholds. No light but the flood beam on her forehead, cutting a cone through silt that hadn't moved in fourteen months. She passed a bolt ring set in the wall — an old staging point, divers clipped into for a rest. The carabiner still hung there, gate sprung open, rope rotted to dust.

*Someone clipped in here. They stopped. They breathed.*

Thirty-three. Her kick slowed. Not by choice. Her legs felt heavy, disconnected, the way they did when the bad air hit the blood and the muscles forgot how to fire. She forced the next kick. The next. The rebreather's solenoid clicked, adding oxygen she couldn't use because the canister wasn't stripping the poison out.

*Come on. Come on.*

Thirty-four. The beam caught something ahead — a pallet, plastic and barnacled, sitting on a concrete shelf that jutted from the shaft wall like a broken tooth. Strapped to it: a case. Military issue, olive drab, corners crushed. Beside it, a smaller bundle wrapped in oilcloth, tied with cord that hadn't rotted.

*The cache. Right there.*

Thirty-five. She reached for the pallet, gloves closing on cold plastic, and the world tilted.

Not the current. Not the surge. Her own body — vision graying at the edges, ears ringing with a sound like a held breath. The CO2 hit the threshold where the brain stops polite and starts shouting. *Breathe. Breathe now. Bigger. Harder.*

She gasped, sucking hard through the mouthpiece, and the canister gave her nothing but resistance. Wet, hot, foul. Her diaphragm spasmed. Again. The gray edge crept inward.

*Thirty-six meters. Eight meters from the surface. Eight meters from air that works.*

She clipped her carabiner to the pallet's D-ring with shaking hands, not trusting her grip. The case's latch was corroded but gave under thumb pressure. Inside: bricks. Gold-colored, stamped, heavy as anchors. Mint. Pre-drown. She didn't count them. Couldn't. Numbers had gone slippery.

The oilcloth bundle was lighter. She tore the cord with her teeth, unwrapped it, and the flood beam caught wool — navy blue, small, a child's coat with a hood and toggle fasteners. The collar was lined with fur gone brittle. A name tag stitched inside: *Teo V.*

Her brother's coat. The one Mara had put him in before sealing the cold-case. The one Nia had never seen again.

The gray closed to a tunnel. Her chest heaved against the mouthpiece, sucking nothing, giving nothing back. The line tugged at her harness — *three sharp pulls, the signal for trouble* — but she couldn't make her thumb find the comms stud. Couldn't remember which button. Couldn't remember *up*.

The last thing she saw before the tunnel pinched shut was the coat floating loose from her numb fingers, drifting down the shaft into dark, and the gold bricks sitting on their pallet, worth berths, worth freedom, worth nothing at all if she didn't kick.

*Kick.*

Her fins moved. Once. Twice. The line went taut. The drum above groaned.
